title: How do I compute operating thresholds for FAR=0% when evaluating biometric match scores in Python/MATLAB?
text:
How do I compute operating thresholds for FAR=0% when evaluating biometric match scores in Python/MATLAB?

I am evaluating a biometric verification system using standard similarity match scores for genuine and impostor comparison distributions. I need to compute the operational decision threshold corresponding to a False Acceptance Rate (FAR) of 0% ($\text{FAR} = 0\%$), where no impostor scores exceed the threshold. Given two 1D NumPy arrays of match scores— genuine_scores and impostor_scores —how can I algorithmically calculate this strict threshold and extract the corresponding False Rejection Rate (FRR) at this zero-FAR operating point in Python? Sample Data Setup: import numpy as np # Simulated match scores (higher score = higher similarity) np.random.seed(42) genuine_scores = np.random.normal(loc=0.8, scale=0.1, size=1000) impostor_scores = np.random.normal(loc=0.3, scale=0.1, size=1000)

title: Retrieve parameters of a redirected website on aiohttp
text:
Retrieve parameters of a redirected website on aiohttp

The code below contains a asynchronous def that sends a request to a OAuth2 server endpoint and when the server returns 200 , the client is redirected to the given redirect point called redirect_uri which is inside of params and inserts two parameters at the url which are code and state ( state is optional based off the API's official documents). async def get_access_token(self, refreshing): async with self.session.get("oauth2 api endpoint", params={ "response_type": "code", "client_id": self.client_id, "redirect_uri": "https://example.com" # << Redirected automatically to this when the response is 200. }, headers={ "Content-Type": "application/json", "User-Agents": "api/v0.0.1a" }) as response: self.__log(response.url, "info") if response.status == 200: self.access_token = response.url.query.get("code") # << Get code paramater here return self.access_token else: self.__log(f"Server returned {response.status} and {response.json if not response.text else response.text}.", "err") The main issue here is that the response.url doesn't change to redirect_uri to retrieve the parameters using url.query.get on the code but it's root API page. Example: GET >> "https://api.web/login" >> if 200 >> "https://redirecting.url/?code=placeholder&state=placeholder" >> but instead >> "https://api.web/onboarding" == the value for response.url (Disclaimer: this code belongs into a class , which explains why there's self and a private function being called in this function and it can be ignored)

title: Import hook at the AST level

title: Python can't find function from imported module - first time creating an __init__.py file
text:
Python can't find function from imported module - first time creating an __init__.py file

I'm trying to better organize a long program I'm working on. In main.py I have this line: from core import * . There is a subfolder called core and in that folder I created a bunch of modules to organize my functions. One is called fileManagement.py . It has a couple functions in it including importInputs() . I also created an __init__.py file in the core folder with __all__ = ["fileManagement"] . Main.py includes this line: df=importInputs() . All of this worked when everything was in one .py file, but now I get NameError: name 'importInputs' is not defined . If I move fileManagement.py to the same directory as main.py , the problem goes away. I've read other posts, such as this one , that discuss adding to the PYTHONPATH. But in researching that, other threads elsewhere say it's not something that generally needs to be edited. Can someone clarify? EDIT: folder structure: main.py core/ __init__.py fileManagement.py To simplify things, I reduced the code to a minimum: main.py: from core import * df = importInputs() core\init.py: __all__ = ["fileManagement"] core\fileManagement.py: def importInputs(): print("Hi") That's it. If I move fileManagement.py into the same directory as main.py, and replace from core import * with from fileManagement import importInputs it works.

title: Pydantic v2: default a generic Literal discriminator from its type parameter
text:
Pydantic v2: default a generic Literal discriminator from its type parameter

I have a generic event base where the discriminator is a type parameter so subclasses don’t redeclare kind : from typing import Annotated, Generic, Literal, TypeVar, Union from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter K = TypeVar("K", bound=str) T = TypeVar("T") class Event(BaseModel, Generic[K, T]): kind: K data: T class Click(BaseModel): x: int y: int class Key(BaseModel): code: str class ClickEvent(Event[Literal["click"], Click]): pass class KeyEvent(Event[Literal["key"], Key]): pass AnyEvent = Annotated[Union[ClickEvent, KeyEvent], Field(discriminator="kind")] print(TypeAdapter(AnyEvent).validate_python({"kind": "key", "data": {"code": "Enter"}})) print(ClickEvent(data={"x": 1, "y": 2})) Validating through the union works: kind='key' data=Key(code='Enter') Constructing the subclass directly fails: Exit code 1 pydantic 2.13.5 pydantic_core 2.46.5 kind='key' data=Key(code='Enter') Traceback (most recent call last): File "/tmp/t.py", line 24, in <module> print(ClickEvent(data={"x": 1, "y": 2})) ~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "/usr/local/lib/python3.13/dist-packages/pydantic/main.py", line 263, in __init__ validated_self = self.__pydantic_validator__.validate_python(data, self_instance=self) pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ClickEvent kind Field required [type=missing, input_value={'data': {'x': 1, 'y': 2}}, input_type=dict] For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/missing kind can only be "click" so I expect pydantic to fill it in. The only fix I found is redeclaring kind: Literal["click"] = "click" in every subclass, which is what the generic was meant to avoid. This works but it mutates model_fields and forces a rebuild: @classmethod def __pydantic_init_subclass__(cls, **kw): super().__pydantic_init_subclass__(**kw) args = get_args(cls.model_fields["kind"].annotation) if args: cls.model_fields["kind"].default = args[0] cls.model_rebuild(force=True) Is there a supported way to derive a field default from a Literal type argument or is redeclaring it per subclass the intended pattern?

title: How to implement RK45 algorithm for N-body simulation
text:
How to implement RK45 algorithm for N-body simulation

I am attempting to write a program that simulates the three-body problem using RK45 (or Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg) integration, following the outline given here PDF I am ultimately trying to use RK45 to simulate a model of the solar system for use in calculating space probe trajectories, but am having trouble implementing RK45 for an N-body system. My program won't calculate the new state of the system and gets stuck in an infinite loop doing so, and I am unsure how to resolve it given how I've written my code (shown below): import numpy as np from matplotlib import pyplot as plt time_val=0 n=0 softening = 5e-5 big_G = 1 max_step = 1e-4 min_step = 1e-10 err_tolerance = 1e-3 state_arr=[ [1, -1.000000000000, 0.000000000000, 0.151837333844, 0.139577137808], [0.6123560888279949, 0.000000000000, 0.000000000000, -0.495911893796, -0.455869192302], [1, 1.000000000000, 0.000000000000, 0.151837333844, 0.139577137808] ] plot_title = 'GOLDEN PANCAKE DRAMA' delta_t = 1e-3 duration_t = 8.8457131110 def arr_calc(inp_arr, index): tot_acc_x = 0 tot_acc_y = 0 x1, y1, vx, vy = inp_arr for i in range(len(state_arr)): if i != index: m, x2, y2 = state_arr[i][:3] rx = x1 - x2 ry = y1 - y2 r_mag_sqr = rx**2 + ry**2 + softening**2 tot_acc_x -= big_G*m*(x1 - x2)/(r_mag_sqr**1.5) tot_acc_y -= big_G*m*(y1 - y2)/(r_mag_sqr**1.5) return np.array([vx, vy, tot_acc_x, tot_acc_y]) def rk45_i(inp_arr, dt, index): r_v_arr = inp_arr[index][1:] k1 = arr_calc(r_v_arr, index)*dt k2 = arr_calc(r_v_arr + k1/4, index)*dt k3 = arr_calc(r_v_arr + k1*3/32 + k2*9/32, index)*dt k4 = arr_calc(r_v_arr + k1*1932/2197 - k2*7200/2197 + k3*7296/2197, index)*dt k5 = arr_calc(r_v_arr + k1*439/216 - k2*8 + k3*3680/513 - k4*845/4104, index)*dt k6 = arr_calc(r_v_arr - k1*8/27 + k2*2 - k3*3544/2565 + k4*1859/4104 - k5*11/40, index)*dt k = k1*25/216 + k2*1408/2625 + k4*2197/4104 - k5*1/5 r = np.abs(k1*1/360 - k3*128/4275 - k4*2197/4104 + k5*1/50 + k6*2/55)/dt return [k, float(max(r))] def rk45_step(inp_arr, dt, err_tol, max_h, min_h): out_arr = inp_arr while True: R_list = [] k_list = [] for i in range(len(inp_arr)): k, r = rk45_i(inp_arr, dt, i) R_list.append(r) k_list.append(k) r_val = max(R_list) delta = 0.84*(err_tol/r_val)**(1/4) print(r_val, err_tol, delta, dt) if delta <= 0.1: dt /= 10 elif delta >= 4: dt *= 4 else: dt *= delta if dt > max_h: dt = max_h elif dt < min_h: dt = min_h if r_val <= err_tol: for i in range(len(inp_arr)): out_arr[i][1:] += k_list[i] return out_arr, dt x1_plot = [] y1_plot = [] x2_plot = [] y2_plot = [] x3_plot = [] y3_plot = [] t_plot = [] frame_interval = 5e2 while time_val < duration_t: state_arr, delta_t = rk45_step(state_arr, delta_t, err_tolerance, max_step, min_step) if n % frame_interval == 0: t_plot.append(time_val) x1_plot.append(state_arr[0][1]) y1_plot.append(state_arr[0][2]) x2_plot.append(state_arr[1][1]) y2_plot.append(state_arr[1][2]) x3_plot.append(state_arr[2][1]) y3_plot.append(state_arr[2][2]) print(f'TRAJECTORY CALCULATION: {round(100*time_val / duration_t, 3):.3f}%') time_val += delta_t n += 1 f=plt.figure(layout='constrained', figsize=(5,5)) plt.plot(x1_plot, y1_plot, c='blue', linewidth=0.25, label='m1') plt.plot(x2_plot, y2_plot, c='red', linewidth=0.25, label='m2') plt.plot(x3_plot, y3_plot, c='green', linewidth=0.25, label='m3') f.legend(loc='outside lower center', fontsize=9, ncols=len(state_arr)+20) plt.show() The periodic solution it is trying to obtain is "Golden Pancake Drama", found here , which I chose due to the various close passes each body makes. For the record, I am aware that SciPy's solve_ivp exists , and that there are methods probably better suited for this purpose. title: QGraphicsScene subclass will not add items which reimplement QGraphicsItem.itemChange, due to diamond-inherited QGraphicsScene subclass
text:
QGraphicsScene subclass will not add items which reimplement QGraphicsItem.itemChange, due to diamond-inherited QGraphicsScene subclass

QGraphicsScene subclass will not add items which reimplement QGraphicsItem.itemChange , due to QGraphicsScene subclass which inherits QGraphicsScene twice. This is not allowed in C++/Qt, its the diamond inheritance problem. I subclass QGraphicsScene in two classes, SceneA and DiamondScene . class SceneA(QGraphicsScene): ... class DiamondScene(SceneA, QGraphicsScene): ... Note that DiamondScene inherits QGraphicsScene twice; the diamond inheritance problem. Question one: why didn't my diamond inheritance scene throw an error? Also, I reimplement ItemChangeRect.itemChange . All it does is call super().itemChange() . The default implementation of itemChange() "does nothing, and returns value". However, the mere presence of this reimplementation of itemChange , when combined with the diamond inheritance scene, has the effect that itemChangeRect will not be added to scene.items() when I call scene.addItem(itemChangeRect) . When I stop inheriting QGraphicsScene twice in my inheritance chain, items which reimplement itemChange() are added to the scene as normal. Question two: Why does the diamond scene seem to work, until I try to add items which have reimplemented QGraphicsItem.itemChange() ? from PySide6.QtWidgets import * from PySide6.QtCore import * from PySide6.QtGui import * import sys class ItemChangeRect(QGraphicsRectItem): def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) self.setFlags(QGraphicsItem.ItemIsMovable|QGraphicsItem.ItemIsSelectable) def itemChange(self, change, value): #When I reimplement itemChange and use diamondScene, item is not actually added to boardScene.items()... However diamond scene performs normally elsewise, except in this behavior return super().itemChange(change, value) class SceneA(QGraphicsScene): pass class DiamondScene(SceneA, QGraphicsScene): pass app = QApplication(sys.argv) view = QGraphicsView() # scene = QGraphicsScene() # Comment in to see that This works. Without diamond inheritance, itemChangeRect is added to scene as per normal. scene = DiamondScene() # DiamondScene seems to work, until you add an item which reimplements .itemChange. In fact, itemChangeRect is never even added to scene.items(), despite our call to .addItem(itemChangeRect) view.setScene(scene) magentaRect = QGraphicsRectItem(-10,-10,20,20) # magentaRect.setBrush(Qt.magenta) itemChangeRect = ItemChangeRect(-10,-10,20,20) itemChangeRect.setPos(50,50) scene.addItem(magentaRect) scene.addItem(itemChangeRect) print('SCENE.ITEMS:', len(scene.items()), scene.items()) # We can see that diamond scene never adds the item which reimplemented .itemChange view.show() sys.exit(qApp.exec())

title: How to express a conditionally required parameter in a Pydantic-validated tool/API schema, without losing the upfront schema validation?
text:
How to express a conditionally required parameter in a Pydantic-validated tool/API schema, without losing the upfront schema validation?

I have a function (specifically an MCP tool built with FastMCP, but this is really a Pydantic/JSON Schema question) where one parameter is required in the normal case, but must be optional when a separate flag parameter is set, since in that branch it genuinely doesn't apply. Simplified shape: async def create_payment_instruction( amount: str, payment_purpose: PaymentPurpose, # required normally status_check_key: str | None = None, # when set, payment_purpose is irrelevant ): if status_check_key is not None: return check_status(status_check_key) # payment_purpose must be present from here on The problem: giving payment_purpose a required type annotation makes the schema reject every call missing it, including the legitimate status-check branch where it's never used. The only fix I've found is making it optional ( PaymentPurpose | None = None ) and manually checking, inside the function body, that payment_purpose is not None whenever status_check_key is absent. That works, but now the generated schema (and anything inspecting it, like client-side form generation or docs) reports the field as optional even though it's actually required in the common case. That feels like giving up real validation for a runtime check. Is there an idiomatic way to express this kind of "required unless field X is set" relationship directly in a Pydantic model, for example with model_validator(mode="after") , a discriminated union, or something in JSON Schema's if / then / dependentRequired , so the constraint is visible in the schema itself rather than only enforced after the fact in the function body?

text:

Here is a simplified version of my table. It has two 'calculated' fields: calc1 and calc2 . And there is a method which calculates sums of specified fields: import sqlalchemy as sa from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, column_property from sqlalchemy.ext.hybrid import hybrid_property class TOne(Base): __tablename__ = 'TOne' RecordID: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) Amt1: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column() Amt2: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column() calc1 = column_property(Amt1 - Amt2) @hybrid_property def calc2(self): return self.Amt1 + self.Amt2 @calc2.expression def calc2(cls): return cls.Amt1 + cls.Amt2 @classmethod def get_aggregated(cls, session, *columns): columns_to_select = [ sa.func.sum(c) for c in columns ] return session.execute( sa.select(*columns_to_select) ).one() It works like this: >>> print(TOne.get_aggregated(session, TOne.Amt1, TOne.calc1, TOne.calc2)) (Decimal('10'), Decimal('-15'), Decimal('35')) The object this method returns is of type sqlalchemy.engine.row.Row and the problem is that names of the values of this tuple-looking object are sum_1 , sum_2 and sum_3 . I would prefer the names to correspond to the names of the columns; in this case the names I need are Amt1 , calc_1 and calc_2 . The SQL request this call produces is: SELECT sum([TOne].[Amt1]) AS sum_1, sum([TOne].[Amt1] - [TOne].[Amt2]) AS sum_2, sum([TOne].[Amt1] + [TOne].[Amt2]) AS sum_3 FROM [TOne] I want it to produce SQL request with different labels: SELECT sum([TOne].[Amt1]) AS Amt1, sum([TOne].[Amt1] - [TOne].[Amt2]) AS calc_1, sum([TOne].[Amt1] + [TOne].[Amt2]) AS calc_2 FROM [TOne] In order to achieve this I tried to specify labels like this: class TOne(Base): ..... @classmethod def get_aggregated(cls, session, *columns): columns_to_select = [ sa.func.sum(c).label(c.name) # <- for c in columns ] .... It does work with 'usual' columns, but not with 'calculated' columns. Looks like for calculated columns declared with colum_property I can use c.key instead of c.name but I am not sure if it is a reliable approach and would prefer a way which would work with all three types of columns.

title: How do I safely remove unused asyncio locks without causing duplicate requests?
text:
How do I safely remove unused asyncio locks without causing duplicate requests?

I'm using asyncio.Lock() to prevent multiple requests for the same user from running at the same time. I also want to remove locks when they're no longer needed instead of keeping them in memory indefinitely. Here's a simplified version of what I'm doing: import asyncio locks = {} async def send_request(user_id): print(f"Starting request for {user_id}") await asyncio.sleep(0.5) print(f"Finished request for {user_id}") async def process(user_id): lock = locks.setdefault(user_id, asyncio.Lock()) async with lock: if user_id in locks: del locks[user_id] await send_request(user_id) async def main(): first = asyncio.create_task(process(42)) await asyncio.sleep(0.01) second = asyncio.create_task(process(42)) await asyncio.gather(first, second) asyncio.run(main()) The output is: Starting request for 42 Starting request for 42 Finished request for 42 Finished request for 42 Both requests start before either one finishes, which is what I'm trying to avoid. I understand that deleting the lock from the dictionary doesn't release it for tasks already using it. The issue is that another task can create a new lock for the same user while the old one is still active. How can I safely remove unused locks without allowing two different locks to exist for the same user at the same time? I'd prefer not to keep a lock for every user indefinitely, especially when the number of user IDs can grow over time.

title: How to make two attr.s instances equal each other in this code

How to make two attr.s instances equal each other in this code

I’m using shapely 2.1.2 and attrs 26.1.0, with the classic attr API. I wrote a Rect class to represent a rotated rectangle, but I’m having trouble making two Rect s with different rotations but same final shape to evaluate equal to each other. Minimum Reproducible Example: from typing import Union from functools import cached_property import attr from shapely.geometry import Point, Polygon from shapely.affinity import rotate @attr.s(frozen=True) class Rect: # raw (unrotated) polygon raw_polygon = attr.ib() # type: Polygon # degrees of clockwise rotation about origin to apply rotation = attr.ib(default=0) # type: Union[int, float] # final, rotated polygon @cached_property def polygon(self) -> Polygon: return rotate( self.raw_polygon, -1 * self.rotation, # negative means clockwise self.raw_polygon.centroid ) def __eq__(self, other): if not isinstance(other, type(self)): return NotImplemented return self.polygon == other.polygon def __ne__(self, other): if not isinstance(other, type(self)): return NotImplemented return self.polygon != other.polygon def __hash__(self): return hash(self.polygon) poly = Polygon([(0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 2), (0, 2)]) rect1 = Rect(poly, rotation=0) rect2 = Rect(poly, rotation=360) print(rect1 == rect2) # should be True, because # rotating 0deg is same as 360deg Output: False EDIT 1: As @jonrsharpe noted, the proper Minimum Reproducible Example should just be comparing two Shapely polygons: from shapely import Polygon from shapely.affinity import rotate poly = Polygon([(0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 2), (0, 2)]) rect1 = rotate(poly, -0, poly.centroid) rect2 = rotate(poly, -360, poly.centroid) print(rect1 == rect2) print(rect1.equals(rect2)) Except that prints True : True True So attrs must have something to do with the problem. EDIT 2: People seem to be getting caught on how I need to use mod 360 for rotation, or Polygon.equals instead of == . So here is another example. Run this with the original Rect class: from shapely.affinity import box poly1 = box(-1, -2, 1, 2) rect1 = Rect(poly1, rotation=0) poly2 = box(-2, -1, 2, 1) rect2 = Rect(poly2, rotation=90) print(rect1 == rect2) # expect True, because # the first Rect is just the second # rotated 90 degrees Output: False And without Rect class, just Shapely: poly1 = box(-1, -2, 1, 2) rect1 = rotate(poly1, -0, poly1.centroid) poly2 = box(-2, -1, 2, 1) rect2 = rotate(poly2, -90, poly2.centroid) print(rect1 == rect2) Output: True

title: Why and how does Python treat __new__ differently when called from an instance?
text:
Why and how does Python treat __new__ differently when called from an instance?

The __new__ method is special because its first argument is cls not self . It’s like a classmethod, but since it isn’t decorated by @classmethod , you have to pass the class name explicitly: class Foo: def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs): print(cls) return object.__new__(cls, *args, **kwargs) Foo.__new__() # TypeError: Foo.__new__() missing 1 required positional argument: ‘cls’ Foo.__new__(Foo) # prints <class ‘__main__.Foo’> What confuses me is when I add a __fake_new__ method which is identical to __new__ except for their name : class Foo: def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs): print(cls) return object.__new__(cls, *args, **kwargs) __fake_new__ = __new__ I call them the exact same way (on an instance of Foo this time), expecting same output: f = Foo() print("Testing begins:") f.__new__(Foo) #1 f.__fake_new__(Foo) #2 For #1 it prints the class (as before), but for #2 it prints the object then errors : <class '__main__.Foo'> Testing begins: <class '__main__.Foo'> <__main__.Foo object at 0x7f88deeca6f0> Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/repl297/main.py", line 12, in <module> f.__fake_new__(Foo) File "/home/repl297/main.py", line 5, in __new__ return object.__new__(cls, *args, **kwargs) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ TypeError: object.__new__(X): X is not a type object (Foo) __new__ and __fake_new__ are identical . What is happening? Why and how does Python treat the first name differently from the second? Do other “special” methods like __class_getitem__ or __prepare__ behave similarly? And if I print args and kwargs too: class Foo: def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs): print(cls, args, kwargs) return object.__new__(cls, *args, **kwargs) __fake_new__ = __new__ f = Foo() print("Testing begins:") f.__new__(Foo) f.__fake_new__(Foo) Output: <class '__main__.Foo'> () {} Testing begins: <class '__main__.Foo'> () {} <__main__.Foo object at 0x7ff40039e750> (<class '__main__.Foo'>,) {} Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/repl411/main.py", line 12, in <module> f.__fake_new__(Foo) File "/home/repl411/main.py", line 5, in __new__ return object.__new__(cls, *args, **kwargs) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ TypeError: object.__new__(X): X is not a type object (Foo) It turns out that for __fake_new__ , self is passed as arg 1, followed by Foo ! <__main__.Foo object at 0x7ff40039e750> (<class '__main__.Foo'>,) {} Whereas for __new__ , only Foo is passed. __new__ acts a bit like a staticmethod in that respect. Why?

title: Python multiprocessing (pool, imap) performance degradation on Linux host
text:
Python multiprocessing (pool, imap) performance degradation on Linux host

Anybody notice a slowdown in multiprocessing pool map/imap after recent Ubuntu or other distro kernel updates? I have a piece of code that was performing a trillion coin toss simulations & analysis on an ancient MacBook Pro on 4 cores (of 8 total) within 90 minutes, but as of a week or two ago, the same code is now taking up to 140 minutes for the same trillion tasks on the same number of cores. Code sample is an overview - the actual code does a variety of simple integer manipulations to tally the results of each run and across runs so that large multi-run jobs are statistically equivalent to single run jobs of the same total number of tosses. Numba should be installed for code to run as intended (to run without, comment out '@jit' decorator, but expect ~100x longer run times). See 'main' code for settings; run count is collected via CLI upon job launch. # Coin Toss Multiprocessing Overview (Simplified) # user configures job/run dimensions & number of processors to engage via CLI # typical midsize test job: 480 runs of 250,000,000 tosses/run for 120B total tosses # (typical production job: 9,600 runs of 250,000,000 tosses/run for 2.2T total tosses) # maxtasksperchild ('mtcp'): [configurable below - currently seeing some improvement with mtpc = 10] # first few run times always include program load overhead # MODULES import multiprocessing as mp # noqa: I001 import random import time from numba import jit # (requires install of Numba to project venv) # Worker process @jit # Numba decorator --> pre-compile loop code def worker_loop(r, n, last_toss): # perform a run (task) heads = 0 tails = 0 # Toss & count for i in range (n): toss = random.randrange(0, 2) if toss: # heads heads += 1 else: tails += 1 return (r, heads, tails) # Stage 2 - Dispatch tasks (runs) to workers in pool def mp_run_spooler(r): run_start = time.time() # 'r' = runs to be done; 'n' = coin tosses/run; 'last_toss' = binary from prior run result = worker_loop(r, n, last_toss) # engage worker process on a run # typical performance at start of job is about 5 seconds/billion tosses # typical performance by end of job is about 9 sec/billion tosses # before issue arose, was seeing 5-6 seconds/billion tosses for whole job # results suggest the RNG is a bottleneck/possible perf issue source loop_time = {time.time() - run_start} result_adj = (*result, *loop_time) return result_adj # Stage 1 - Activate pool def mp_pooler(runs, cpu_mp): global best_sec_toss # usually seen a few runs into the job global prior_sec_toss with mp.Pool(cpu_mp, maxtasksperchild=mtcp) as pool: # Dispatch runs to Stage 2, receive returns for result in pool.imap(mp_run_spooler, range(runs)): print(f"run {result[0] + 1}/{runs:,} heads: {result[1]:,} tails: {result[2]:,} run time: {result[3]:,}") time_toss = (time.time() - start) / ((result[0] + 1) * n) # avg job time so far if result[0] == 0: # first run best_sec_toss = time_toss else: best_sec_toss = min(best_sec_toss, prior_sec_toss) # following runs if (result[0] + 1) % cpu_mp == 0: # run number is multiple of processors engaged print(f"
 best sec/toss: {best_sec_toss}\ 
current sec/toss: {time_toss} ({(result[0] + 1) * n:,} tosses)\ 
 perf trend: {(time_toss / best_sec_toss -1) * -100:.1f}% (avg job time/toss vs. best run time/toss)
") prior_sec_toss = time_toss # set up for next # Main app if __name__ == "__main__": # prod app uses CLI menu to initialize/collect user settings, then a variety of # bespoke functions to support job launch & i/o orchestration runs = int(input("
enter runs: ")) # use value giving 60-180 sec overall job time n = 500000000 # increase/lower to adjust task sizes last_toss = 0 # irrelevant here, but carried over to simulate app's variable passing cpu_mp = 4 # processors/cores to be engaged mtcp = 10 # maxtasksperchild in best_sec_toss = 0 prior_sec_toss = 0 print("
working...
") start = time.time() mp_pooler(runs, cpu_mp) # up to Stage 1 I'm seeing a steady decline in performance as long jobs execute. They start with a ~70% boost over single-processor mode using 4 cores, then drops to about a 50% gain by end of job. Processor load seems to drop off as well - the fans used to run whole job, now they calm after 15-20 mins or so & the system monitor shows a coincident drop in processor load percentages. In single-processor mode, I continue to see stable performance in line with prior expectations and results. My project is running in a venv, Python 3.12.3. The host is the MacBook Pro mentioned above (early 2013), now running Ubuntu 24.04 (current via Software Updater daily check). I've made no changes to the host, the venv or the code in the last while that I can pin this against. I see the same behaviour with or without other apps (browser, etc.) running. I'm currently giving maxtasksperchild a trial as it seems to fit my architecture (playing with chunksize --> no joy), results still inconclusive - maybe a mild performance bump, but not back to where things were. I'm wondering if something maybe changed in the last while down in the OS guts, but no idea what that might be. Hence asking here if anyone else has seen similar when running similar code.

Consider this file foo.py in VS Code: from .bar import baz # local import PI = 3.14 class Foo: def bar: pass def hello(): pass How can I launch the following session? >>> 'baz' in globals() True >>> 'PI' in globals() True >>> 'Foo' in globals() True >>> 'hello' in globals() True >>> # Continue testing all these objects interactively Obviously, I could just test inside an ifmain guard in the file: if __main__ == ‘__name__’: # do testing here Then every time I want to play with something else, I could update the code under the if-statement, save the file, and run the file. However, that’s repetitive, and not interactive. Moreover, I was once programming a small bot running Ev3dev, and it took over 40 secs just to import ev3dev2 . It was infeasible to rerun the file every time and wait 40 seconds just to test something new or make an adjustment to the code. In that situation, I would have liked to run the file (which contained, say, a Robot class) once on the bot, then opened up a REPL session through VS Code: >>> r = Robot() >>> r.drive(10) # test different movements >>> r.turn(45) >>> Robot.OFFSET += 5 # adjust a constant >>> r.turn(45) # test again Is there such a feature in VS Code?

title: Write a typing.Protocol when its implementations have different arg names
text:
Write a typing.Protocol when its implementations have different arg names

I want to write a SupportsPut protocol that defines an abstract method named put . It should allow multiprocessing.Queue.put and queue.Queue.put of the standard library as valid implementations. However, looking at the source, they have an argument name mismatch ( obj vs. item ): # in multiprocessing.Queue: def put(self, obj, block=True, timeout=None): ... # in queue.Queue: def put(self, item, block=True, timeout=None): ... So if I try to make them both SupportsPut s, I can only choose either obj or item as the protocol method argument: class SupportsPut(Protocol): def put(self, item, block=True, timeout=None): ... If I test it: def do_something_with(thing: SupportsPut): thing.put("hello") do_something_with(mp.Queue()) # <- do_something_with(q.Queue()) I get as expected a Pylance error that mp.Queue.put doesn’t conform to the protocol’s put . In the snippet, do_something_with() treats the first argument positionally, by calling .put("hello") instead of .put(obj="hello") or put(item="hello") , thus avoiding the name conflict. However, SupportsPut.put must choose one of the two names. Is allowing both signatures proper duck typing? If the protocol were @runtime_checkable , what would it make sense for isinstance(mp.Queue(), SupportsPut) to return? How should I write the Protocol so that both Pylance and isinstance() are satisfied? This argument name mismatch is just one example of accounting for slight variations in implementation signatures. In most cases the variation can be resolved by sticking to what fits both, as shown above. Examples: # two implementations: def foo(self, val: Any): ... def foo(self, val: int): ... # can be resolved by passing only an int: thing_that_supports_foo.foo(42) def foo(self, **kwargs): ... def foo(self): ... # can be resolved by not passing extra kwargs: thing_that_supports_foo.foo() Is there a general method of writing a Protocol for these situations?

title: Detecting keypress and keyrelease on arrow keys
text:
Detecting keypress and keyrelease on arrow keys

I'm making a video player in which I can use the right / left arrow keys to skip the video forward / backward 5 seconds. This was simple enough to do initially using QShortcuts , but I wanted to develop it to keep skipping the video while the key is held down. This became sluggish, so I used a short QTimer to debounce setting the video position, but then ran into the problem that while the video was still playing, it would jump back to its playing position while I'm doing the skipping. So, my problem is, I want to pause the video when the arrow key is first pressed, keep skipping while it auto-repeats, and resume playing when the key is released. My first go at this was to use an eventFilter . This didn't work because the KeyPress events were moving the focus between the child widgets and were never reaching my eventFilter , although the KeyRelease events were. This was where my original question came from - turned out I was misunderstanding eventFilters , I thought they intercepted events before they reached the child widgets. An answer on the original question which has now been deleted, suggested installing eventFilter on the QApplication instead. This worked, but I was advised to avoid this, and realised I would run into problems with the eventFilter catching key events for every window in my actual app. On closer testing when I was putting this question together, I also found that KeyRelease event was happening after every time the KeyPress auto-repeated, even though the key hadn't been released. Original code using eventFilter : import os import datetime from PyQt6 import QtCore, QtGui, QtWidgets, QtMultimedia, QtMultimediaWidgets class VideoPlayer(QtWidgets.QWidget): def __init__(self, path): super().__init__() self.resize(800,600) self.setWindowTitle(os.path.basename(path)) self.media_player = QtMultimedia.QMediaPlayer() self.media_player.setSource(QtCore.QUrl.fromLocalFile(path)) self.media_player.positionChanged.connect(self.setSeekBarPosition) self.media_player.durationChanged.connect(self.setDuration) self.media_player.playbackStateChanged.connect(self.setPlayPauseButton) self.video_widget = QtMultimediaWidgets.QVideoWidget() self.video_widget.setSizePolicy(QtWidgets.QSizePolicy.Policy.Expanding, QtWidgets.QSizePolicy.Policy.Expanding) self.media_player.setVideoOutput(self.video_widget) self.play_pause_btn = QtWidgets.QPushButton(QtGui.QIcon(self.style().standardIcon(QtWidgets.QStyle.StandardPixmap.SP_MediaPlay)), "") self.play_pause_btn.clicked.connect(self.togglePlayPause) self.position_lbl = QtWidgets.QLabel("0:00:00") self.seek_bar = QtWidgets.QSlider(QtCore.Qt.Orientation.Horizontal) self.seek_bar.setSizePolicy(QtWidgets.QSizePolicy.Policy.Expanding, QtWidgets.QSizePolicy.Policy.Minimum) self.duration_lbl = QtWidgets.QLabel("0:00:00") controls_layout = QtWidgets.QHBoxLayout() controls_layout.addWidget(self.play_pause_btn) controls_layout.addWidget(self.position_lbl) controls_layout.addWidget(self.seek_bar) controls_layout.addWidget(self.duration_lbl) main_layout = QtWidgets.QVBoxLayout(self) main_layout.setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0) main_layout.addWidget(self.video_widget) main_layout.addLayout(controls_layout) play_pause_shortcut = QtGui.QShortcut(QtGui.QKeySequence("space"), self) play_pause_shortcut.activated.connect(self.togglePlayPause) self.playing_before_skip = False self.key_filter = VideoKeyFilter() self.key_filter.key_pressed.connect(self.skipKeyPressed) self.key_filter.key_released.connect(self.skipKeyReleased) self.key_filter.skip.connect(self.skip) self.installEventFilter(self.key_filter) self.position_debounce_timer = QtCore.QTimer() self.position_debounce_timer.setSingleShot(True) self.position_debounce_timer.setInterval(50) self.position_debounce_timer.timeout.connect(self.setVideoPosition) def setSeekBarPosition(self, position): self.seek_bar.setValue(position) sec = int(position / 1000) self.position_lbl.setText(str(datetime.timedelta(seconds=sec))) def setDuration(self, duration): self.seek_bar.setRange(0, duration) sec = int(duration / 1000) self.duration_lbl.setText(str(datetime.timedelta(seconds=sec))) def setPlayPauseButton(self, state): if state == QtMultimedia.QMediaPlayer.PlaybackState.PlayingState: icon = QtWidgets.QStyle.StandardPixmap.SP_MediaPause else: icon = QtWidgets.QStyle.StandardPixmap.SP_MediaPlay self.play_pause_btn.setIcon(self.style().standardIcon(icon)) def isPlaying(self): return self.media_player.playbackState() == QtMultimedia.QMediaPlayer.PlaybackState.PlayingState def togglePlayPause(self): if self.isPlaying(): self.media_player.pause() else: self.media_player.play() def skipKeyPressed(self): self.playing_before_skip = self.isPlaying() if self.playing_before_skip: self.media_player.pause() def skipKeyReleased(self): if self.playing_before_skip: self.media_player.play() def skip(self, delta): new_position = max(min(self.seek_bar.value() + delta, self.seek_bar.maximum()), 0) self.setSeekBarPosition(new_position) self.position_debounce_timer.start() def setVideoPosition(self): self.media_player.setPosition(self.seek_bar.value()) class VideoKeyFilter(QtCore.QObject): key_pressed = QtCore.pyqtSignal() key_released = QtCore.pyqtSignal() skip = QtCore.pyqtSignal(int) def eventFilter(self, obj, event): if event.type() == QtCore.QEvent.Type.KeyPress: if delta := self.whichKey(event): if not event.isAutoRepeat(): self.key_pressed.emit() self.skip.emit(delta) return True if event.type() == QtCore.QEvent.Type.KeyRelease: if delta := self.whichKey(event): self.key_released.emit() return True return False def whichKey(self, event): # Returns how many milliseconds to move the video position, # depending on which key was pressed if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_Right: return 5000 if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_Left: return -5000 return None if __name__=="__main__": app = QtWidgets.QApplication([]) player = VideoPlayer("path_to_some_video.mp4") player.show() app.exec()

title: What kind of regular expression captures the root of a URL?
text:
What kind of regular expression captures the root of a URL?

Consider the following examples of URLs: URL Root https://fr-wiktionary-org.translate.goog/wiki/s translate.goog https://python.regex.parse.smackoverflow.net/questions/answer smackoverflow.net www.linkedout.com/out/jane-doe linkedout.com http://www.linkedout.com/out/jane-doe linkedout.com https://www.linkedout.com/out/jane-doe linkedout.com The root of a URL is always of the form something.something . The root contains the right-most dot ( . ) that is to the left of the forward slashes ( / ), except for the forward slashes ( / ) inside of https:// . What Python regular expression will place the root of a URL inside of a capturing group, and discard the other parts of the URL? The following regex almost works: (?:https?:\/\/)??(?:[0-9a-zA-Z-\.])*\.([0-9a-zA-Z-]+\.[0-9a-zA-Z-]+){1}(?:[0-9a-zA-Z-\/]*) Regex101 If the capturing group for root of the URL is lazy instead of greedy, then we have bad results for the root capturing group, such as e.g , instead of translate.goog . The root of a URL is similar to, but not the same as, the longest possible sub-string of the URL that includes exactly one dot . (not two dots, or three dots, etc.) and such that our sub-string of interest does not contain any forward slashes / .

title: Where is the Python documentation for handling ties with the built-in min function?
text:
Where is the Python documentation for handling ties with the built-in min function?

I was doing an exercise where I need to get the closest value to a given target in a binary search tree (BST) and, this is important, return the lower number in case of a tie . The solution provided this code snippet. This means that if the BST has 3 and 4 and the target is 3.5, because the two 0.5 from the target, we should return 3 and not 4. This is a test case that I initially failed. closest = min(closest, curr.val, key=lambda x: (abs(x-target), x)) Here's the full code: def closestValue(root: TreeNode, target: float) -> int: if not root: return None curr = root closest = root.val while curr: closest = min(closest, curr.val, key=lambda x: (abs(x-target), x)) if target < curr.val: curr = curr.left else: curr = curr.right return closest What I didn't understand about the code snippet was how the key handled the tuple provided in the lambda. I looked at the documentation and couldn't find the explanation. See the quoted sections of the Python documentation that just stated that they pick the "first encountered". When I asked Gemini Flash: What does this code do with the tuple in the lambda? closest = min(root.val, closest, key = lambda x: (abs(target - x), x) I got an answer that referred to the exact failed test case of 3 and 4 with target 3.5. The tuple (abs(target - x), x) is used by Python's min() function as a multi-level sorting key (lexicographical comparison) to resolve ties. Here is how Python evaluates it for each value x : Primary Key — abs(target - x) : min() first compares the first element of the tuple. The value of x that is closest to target (smallest absolute distance) wins. Tie-Breaker — x : If both values are equidistant from target (e.g., target = 3.5 , with candidate values 3 and 4 , where both have abs(target - x) == 0.5 ), Python falls back to comparing the second element of the tuple. Because standard min() looks for the smaller value, it picks the smaller candidate x (in that scenario, 3 ). This pattern is the standard Python idiom for finding the closest value to a target while ensuring deterministic tie-breaking (favoring the smaller value). The sources mentioned in Gemini aren't valid, so where in the documentation is this behavior mentioned? I couldn't find it in min's documentation and even checked max in case the documentation was meant to avoid duplication but it is not explained there either. min ( iterable , / , * , key=None ) ¶ min ( iterable , / , * , default , key=None ) min ( arg1 , arg2 , / , *args , key=None ) Return the smallest item in an iterable or the smallest of two or more arguments. If one positional argument is provided, it should be an iterable . The smallest item in the iterable is returned. If two or more positional arguments are provided, the smallest of the positional arguments is returned. There are two optional keyword-only arguments. The key argument specifies a one-argument ordering function like that used for list.sort() . The default argument specifies an object to return if the provided iterable is empty. If the iterable is empty and default is not provided, a ValueError is raised. If multiple items are minimal, the function returns the first one encountered. This is consistent with other sort-stability preserving tools such as sorted(iterable, key=keyfunc)[0] and heapq.nsmallest(1, iterable, key=keyfunc) . Changed in version 3.4: Added the default keyword-only parameter. Changed in version 3.8: The key can be None .

title: How to catch keypress event on arrow keys, and stop them from moving focus?
text:
How to catch keypress event on arrow keys, and stop them from moving focus?

I'm trying to catch keypress and keyrelease events on the arrow keys in a QWidget to perform some actions. At first I used QShortcuts, this worked, but I want to develop it further to do some action when the key is pressed down, but not repeat the action if the key is held down, then do something else when it's released. I'm learning how to use eventFilter to do this. I've made the below cut-down example: from PyQt6 import QtWidgets, QtCore class MyWindow(QtWidgets.QWidget): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.resize(500,300) vbox = QtWidgets.QVBoxLayout(self) vbox.addWidget(QtWidgets.QPushButton("A Button")) vbox.addWidget(QtWidgets.QPushButton("Another Button")) self.text_box = QtWidgets.QPlainTextEdit() self.text_box.setSizePolicy(QtWidgets.QSizePolicy.Policy.Expanding, QtWidgets.QSizePolicy.Policy.Expanding) vbox.addWidget(self.text_box) self.setFocusPolicy(QtCore.Qt.FocusPolicy.StrongFocus) self.key_filter = KeyFilter() self.key_filter.key_pressed.connect(self.keyPressed) self.key_filter.key_released.connect(self.keyReleased) self.installEventFilter(self.key_filter) def keyPressed(self, key): self.text_box.appendPlainText("KeyPress - " + key) self.text_box.verticalScrollBar().setValue(self.text_box.verticalScrollBar().maximum()) def keyReleased(self, key): self.text_box.appendPlainText("KeyRelease - " + key) self.text_box.verticalScrollBar().setValue(self.text_box.verticalScrollBar().maximum()) class KeyFilter(QtCore.QObject): key_pressed = QtCore.pyqtSignal(str) key_released = QtCore.pyqtSignal(str) def eventFilter(self, obj, event): if event.type() == QtCore.QEvent.Type.KeyPress: if key := self.whichKey(event): self.key_pressed.emit(key) return True if event.type() == QtCore.QEvent.Type.KeyRelease: if key := self.whichKey(event): self.key_released.emit(key) return True return False def whichKey(self, event): if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_A: return "A" if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_Left: return "left" if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_Right: return "right" if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_Up: return "up" if event.key() == QtCore.Qt.Key.Key_Down: return "down" return None if __name__ == "__main__": app = QtWidgets.QApplication([]) win = MyWindow() win.show() app.exec() The problems I've got are: the arrow keys move the focus between the buttons and text box - I thought installing an eventFilter and returning True was supposed to stop any default action? I've tried adding event.accept() before the return but it made no difference. the KeyPress is never shown for the arrow keys, only the KeyRelease. I get KeyPress and KeyRelease for the "A" key (except if the QPlainTextEdit has focus, then I only get KeyRelease). I figure the buttons are blocking the KeyPress (and the text box is absorbing KeyPress on the "A" key), but again I thought an eventFilter got the events before the child widgets. I know I can stop the buttons & text box receiving focus with setFocusPolicy(QtCore.Qt.FocusPolicy.NoFocus) but: I don't want to have to set this on every child widget I still want to be able to use Tab to move between them, but not the arrow keys.

title: How to add a method to a specific instance in Python
text:
How to add a method to a specific instance in Python

In this example: >>> class Foo: pass >>> obj = Foo() How can I add a method to obj ? >>> obj.meth() #as an example,meth() does print(self) <__main__.Foo object at 0xfff> I’ve tried: >>> obj.meth = lambda self: print(self) >>> obj.meth() (TypeError) Which fails because self isn’t magically removed from the signature. Adding it to the class works: >>> Foo.meth = lambda self: print(self) >>> obj.meth() <__main__.Foo object at 0xfff> Because the method’s signature is reduced, as inspect shows: >>> def num_args(func): return len(inspect.signature(func).parameters) >>> num_args(Foo.meth) 1 >>> num_args(obj.meth) 0 But adding a method to the class adds it to the method lookup chain of all Foo instances, not just obj . I can only think of this: >>> obj.meth = lambda obj=obj: print(obj) >>> obj.meth() <__main__.Foo object at 0xfff> The drawback is that the reference to obj makes the lambda hard to pass around and apply to different objects. Is this the correct way to add a method to an instance?

title: NGBoost multi-step ahead probabilistic forecasting for 96 time steps
text:
NGBoost multi-step ahead probabilistic forecasting for 96 time steps

I am building a probabilistic energy forecasting model using NGBoost ( NGBRegressor ) to predict household residual power ( residual_power_w ) at 15-minute resolution. My goal is to forecast the full next 24 hours (96 steps) with uncertainty estimates (prediction intervals, CRPS) at each step. The problem: NGBoost only supports a scalar target — fit() accepts a 1D array. Unlike XGBoost which has multi_strategy='multi_output_tree' for native multi-output, NGBoost has no equivalent. What I have tried: The NGBoost maintainer on GitHub Discussion #243 confirmed the only current approach is one model per horizon step: "At the moment there isn't a simple way to predict all of [yt+1 ... yt+n] in one shot, so you have to use one model for t+1, another model for t+2, and so on up to t+n" So training 96 separate NGBoost models is the documented workaround. However this is very expensive since NGBoost is already slow compared to XGBoost. The MultivariateNormal(k=96) distribution exists in NGBoost but requires k*(k+3)/2 = 4,752 parameters per row — completely impractical for k=96. My question: Is there a better approach to get probabilistic 96-step ahead forecasts from NGBoost without training 96 separate models? Specifically I need: Prediction intervals at each of the 96 horizon steps CRPS evaluation per step Any alternative that keeps the probabilistic output (not just point forecasts) is welcome. Environment: Python 3, ngboost 0.4+, sklearn

title: X-Twilio-Signature validation fails for TwiML App webhook (Voice JS SDK client call, custom params) — verified URL/token/params are all correct
text:
X-Twilio-Signature validation fails for TwiML App webhook (Voice JS SDK client call, custom params) — verified URL/token/params are all correct

I'm getting a persistent 403 "Invalid webhook signature" on my TwiML Application's Voice Request URL webhook, triggered by the Voice JS SDK's device.connect() with custom params. Using twilio-python's official RequestValidator (v9.11.1). I've exhaustively ruled out the usual causes: The exact URL I validate against is byte-identical (SHA-256 compared) to the URL Twilio itself reports in the Console error message ("Got HTTP 403 response to https://..."). The Auth Token I use is byte-identical (SHA-256 compared) to the Primary Auth Token shown on my Account Dashboard (confirmed it's not a leftover Secondary token). Twilio's own "Request Inspector" in the Call Log shows the exact params it sent — they match, field for field, what my server actually received (AccountSid, ApiVersion, ApplicationSid, CallSid, CallStatus, Called, Caller, Direction, From, To, plus one custom param). I brute-forced every one of the 2^11 possible subsets of those 11 received params against the received X-Twilio-Signature using RequestValidator.compute_signature(). None of the 2048 combinations reproduce it. No duplicate form keys, Content-Length matches the received body size. Account is on the IE1 (Ireland) region/edge. Has anyone seen X-Twilio-Signature validation fail specifically for TwiML App webhooks triggered by Client SDK connect() calls carrying custom parameters, despite URL, token, and params all being provably correct? Is there a known difference in how the signature is computed for this call path vs a standard REST-API-initiated call?

text:

Everything works as expected when using standard dataclasses. However, as soon as I enable slots=True (introduced in Python 3.10+) on both the base and mixin classes, Python throws a TypeError: multiple bases have instance lay-out conflict during class creation. from dataclasses import dataclass # Base mixin containing shared tracking state @dataclass(slots=True) class ServiceMixin: service_id: str # Base entity dataclass @dataclass(slots=True) class BaseEntity: entity_id: int # Child class inheriting from both base classes @dataclass(slots=True) class UserEntity(BaseEntity, ServiceMixin): username: str Error: Traceback (most recent call last): File "main.py", line 14, in <module> class UserEntity(BaseEntity, ServiceMixin): TypeError: multiple bases have instance lay-out conflict I tried: Removing slots=True from child or parents. If I set slots=False on ServiceMixin , the exception goes away, but UserEntity falls back to creating a standard __dict__ , which defeats the memory optimization goal. Reordering the base classes. Changing the MRO to class UserEntity(ServiceMixin, BaseEntity) yields the exact same error. Defining empty __slots__ = () manually. If I define ServiceMixin without @dataclass(slots=True) and manually set __slots__ = ('service_id',) or __slots__ = () , the behavior changes unpredictably depending on which parent class declares non-empty slots. How can I safely apply slots=True across multiple inherited dataclasses without triggering CPython's layout conflict restriction? Is there an idiomatic pattern or workaround (e.g., via a helper mixin or metaclass) to allow slot-based multiple inheritance in dataclasses?

title: When and how should __all__ be defined?
text:
When and how should __all__ be defined?

When should a module define __all__ vs using the underscore convention? Should this be done manually or dynamically? Ideally, we could answer this once and for all with 'write it all out manually' and 'explicit is better than implicit', as has been said here . But in reality, cases such as these arise: You are writing an __all__ for the __init__.py in the top level of a package, re-exporting perhaps hundreds of public functions and classes spread across multiple submodules. Now every edit to a nested file requires a trip to every __init__.py file, adding the new string to every __all__ . You are writing an __all__ for a constants.py storing hundreds of config constants. Now every insertion, deletion and modification of a constant has to happen to the __all__ too (two sources of truth). You are defining parts of your API conditionally. For example, maybe a certain class is defined on Windows and not on Linux, or on Python >3.9 only. Or maybe a function is only defined under a try / except / else clause. Or maybe certain functionalities are only available for Pro users. That would require an __all__ += or __all__.append . __all__ is supposed to solve: Pollution of the global namespace (star imports) Readable separation of public/private API But when it is explicitly written out, you get: Harder-to-maintain Less DRY But when it is dynamically generated (e.g. for -loop), you get: Potentially unclear public API Unhappy IDE/linter Some other suggestions: (as mentioned here ) Prepend all unexported names - including modules, helpers, etc - with an underscore, and let the import machinery handle the rest. This is not something I do, because it would make the code less readable and me more annoyed (see the rejected PEP 842's Motivation ). Use the auto-all package as suggested here and here . However, this doesn't seem to be linter-friendly, and would be similar to using a dynamic list comprehension anyway. Don't write __all__ . PEP 8 advises that 'modules should explicitly declare the names in their public API using the __all__ attribute'. However, a github search in CPython yields: __all__ = [x for x in dir(context._default_context) if not x.startswith('_')] # multiprocessing/__init__.py __all__ = [name for name, obj in globals().items() if not name.startswith('_') and not isinstance(obj, types.ModuleType) and name not in {'wantobjects'}] # types.py __all__.append("HTTPSConnection") # http/client.py __all__.append('_exit') # os.py __all__.append('SharedMemoryManager') # multiprocessing/managers.py Writing __all__ dynamically is a common pattern.

title: Why does subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) with shlex.quote() break on Windows?

Why does subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) with shlex.quote() break on Windows?

I'm invoking a CLI tool from Python using: import subprocess, shlex cmd = f'somecli eval {shlex.quote(js_code)}' subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True) This works correctly on Linux/macOS, but on Windows the argument (containing characters like < , > , && , => , backticks) gets mangled — the target CLI reports things like "SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token", even though the exact same command string is correct POSIX shell syntax. I understand shell=True on Windows invokes cmd.exe instead of /bin/sh , and shlex.quote() only produces POSIX-safe quoting. What's the correct, portable way to pass a single arbitrary string argument (containing shell metacharacters) to a subprocess so it survives on both platforms? The fix I ended up using was avoiding the shell entirely — resolving the tool's real executable and calling it via an argv list with shell=False : subprocess.run([resolved_exe, entry_script, *args], shell=False, ...) Is this the recommended approach, or is there a cleaner cross-platform way to keep using shell=True safely?

If I understand correctly, method="trust-constr" is considered to be the most modern, highest-quality, and currently-best-supported of the strategies available for scipy.optimize.minimize() when doing constrained minimization. In particular, it's the only method that supports both constraints and analytic gradient and hessian. But I am having trouble getting reasonable accuracy from it. Its accuracy is low by default (roughly single precision), which is fine, but I haven't succeeded in finding settings to get it much better than that. My simple test example problem is to find the local minimum of y=cos(x) near x=3, with no constraints. That local minimum occurs at x=pi, y=-1. If I'm not mistaken, this example problem is well-conditioned (locally well-approximated by a quadratic), so I expect the solve to go simply and smoothly-- there's not much to it. The larger "real" problems I am trying to solve are similar to this, generally with equality constraints (so this limits which solver strategies I can use; "trust-constr" is one of the few). I often don't have inequality constraints. The objective functions are "nice" in the sense that they have a quadratic basin around the desired local minimum. Further details of my much-more-complicated real-life objective functions and equality constraints aren't relevant here-- the accuracy problem with trust-constr is shown clearly by cos(x) without needing any constraints at all. The program below tries 20 or so different initial guesses between 2.0 and 4.0, with aggressive tolerance settings agnostic to whether there are constraints and/or bounds: gtol,xtol,barrier_tol all set to 1e-20 (the default for all three is 1e-8). The answers from scipy have relative error as high as 3e-9 (i.e. slightly better than single precision accuracy). On this well-conditioned input, I expected something on the order of 1e-15 (double-precision accuracy). For comparison, the program also contains a little Newton's-method solver. Given the same information as was given to scipy.optimize.minimize() (the gradient and hessian, asking it to find where the gradient is zero) the Newton solver always converges to exactly the right answer (to machine precision) math.pi, in 7 or fewer iterations, as expected, on each of the initial guesses. I expect 'trust-constr' to be able to do this too. Am I doing something wrong in my usage of scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') ? I guess I could code up my own constrained-minimizer from first principles using Newton's method and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_multiplier . But I thought scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') was supposed to be a state-of-the-art implementation of that and more... isn't it? title: How to deal with implicit transformation into parent type when using a TypeVar?
text:
How to deal with implicit transformation into parent type when using a TypeVar?

Consider the following code: from __future__ import annotations from typing import Generic, Self, TypeVar, overload T = TypeVar("T", float, complex) class Dummy(Generic[T]): def __init__(self, value: T) -> None: self.value = value @overload def __mul__(self, other: float | T) -> Self: ... @overload def __mul__(self, other: complex) -> Dummy[complex]: ... def __mul__(self, other: float | complex) -> Self | Dummy[complex]: return Dummy(self.value * other) def some_func(self, dummy: Dummy[T]): pass def some_other_func(self, dummy: Dummy[T], other: T): self.some_func(dummy * other) The idea is to replicate the fact that if you multiply a float or a complex by a float, its "nature" doesn't change, but if you multiply by a complex, then you necessarily get a complex. There is one other property that kind of overlaps with this: if you multiply a float or complex by something of the same "nature", its nature also doesn't change. Note that the two definitions of __mul__ don't contradict each other, so it's not immediate to see this: multiplying a Dummy[complex] by a complex could take each branch, both resulting in a Dummy[complex] . However, ty complains about this. Running ty check with the configuration: [tool.ty.rules] unsound-return-statement = "error" unsound-assignment = "error" unsound-yield = "error" missing-type-argument = "error" possibly-unresolved-reference = "error" raises: error[invalid-argument-type]: Argument to bound method `Dummy.some_func` is incorrect --> /tmp/test.py:20:24 | 20 | self.some_func(dummy * other) | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Expected `Dummy[T@Dummy]`, found `Dummy[T@Dummy] | Dummy[complex]` info: element `Dummy[complex]` of union `Dummy[T@Dummy] | Dummy[int | float* | complex*]` is not assignable to `Dummy[T@Dummy]` info: └── element `complex*` of union `int | float* | complex*` is not assignable to `T@Dummy` info: └── type `complex*` is not assignable to any element of the union `int | float*` info: ├── element `complex*` of union `int | float* | complex*` is not assignable to `float` info: └── ... omitted 1 union element without additional context info: Method defined here --> /tmp/test.py:16:9 | 16 | def some_func(self, dummy: Dummy[T]): | ^^^^^^^^^ --------------- Parameter declared here Found 1 diagnostic What is the correct way of dealing with this? How should I change my stubs to carry the facts that: multiplying by a float or the same type T doesn't change the type of the object; and multiplying by a complex transforms it into a complex object?

title: Why can moving an await change whether a Python object remains reachable, even when the object has no explicit strong reference?
text:
Why can moving an await change whether a Python object remains reachable, even when the object has no explicit strong reference?

I am trying to understand a surprising difference in object lifetime in Python asyncio . Consider this simplified example: import asyncio import gc import weakref class Resource: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def __del__(self): print(f"destroyed: {self.name}") async def producer(): resource = Resource("A") reference = weakref.ref(resource) await asyncio.sleep(0) return reference async def main(): reference = await producer() print("before gc:", reference()) gc.collect() print("after gc:", reference()) asyncio.run(main()) Now consider a small variation where the suspension point is moved: async def producer(): resource = Resource("A") reference = weakref.ref(resource) return reference await asyncio.sleep(0) I understand that local variables belong to a coroutine frame and that an await suspends the coroutine rather than creating a normal function call boundary. What I find difficult to reason about is the following: The exact point where resource ceases to be strongly reachable Whether the suspended coroutine frame necessarily retains every local variable When a returned coroutine releases its frame Whether an asyncio.Task can indirectly keep local variables alive through the coroutine object or its frame How that interacts with CPython's reference counting versus cyclic garbage collection Whether the lifetime behavior above guaranteed by Python's language semantics, or whether some of it is specifically an implementation detail of CPython Whether there is a reliable way to inspect the reference chain responsible for keeping resource alive without relying on implementation-specific asyncio internals I am especially interested in the distinction between: Python name ↓ coroutine frame ↓ coroutine object ↓ asyncio.Task ↓ event loop and the actual reference graph that exists while a coroutine is running, suspended, and completed. For debugging I have also tried: print(gc.get_referrers(resource)) but the results are difficult to interpret because the inspection itself creates temporary references and some objects involved in the execution machinery are not obvious from the Python source code. What is the correct mental model for determining the lifetime of a local object captured by a suspended coroutine? Observed behavior When I run the first version, I get: before gc: None destroyed: A after gc: None When I change the position of the await , I get: before gc: <__main__.Resource object at 0x...> after gc: <__main__.Resource object at 0x...> I was not expecting moving the await to change the lifetime of resource , since there is no explicit reference to it outside the coroutine. This is the part I am trying to understand: what reference is keeping the object alive, and how does moving the suspension point change the reference graph?

title: How do I design a multi-purpose event handler without making it generic?
text:
How do I design a multi-purpose event handler without making it generic?

I am trying to design an event handler that can be used by different classes to manage events specific to that class. The event handler doesn't really need to know what type the events are as long as they are an Event subclass (or maybe I could use a Protocol?) Here is a simplified version which has a problem: EventHandler.add_subscription() won't accept a callback that takes a specific class of Event (i.e. a CustomEvent ) even though CustomEvent is a subclass of Event . from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Hashable, Callable, Protocol from abc import ABC @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) class Event(ABC): event_type: Hashable class EventHandler: subs: dict[Hashable, dict[int, Callable[[Event], None]]] _next_id: int def __init__(self) -> None: self.subs = dict() self._next_id = 0 def add_subscription(self, event_type: Hashable, callback: Callable[[Event], None]) -> int: self._next_id += 1 if not event_type in self.subs: self.subs[event_type] = dict() self.subs[event_type][self._next_id] = callback return self._next_id def post_event(self, event: Event): for callback in self.subs[event.event_type].values(): callback(event) @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) class CustomEvent(Event): event_type: int value: float class CustomEventGenerator: event_handler : EventHandler def __init__(self) -> None: self.event_handler = EventHandler() def emit_event(self, value: float): self.event_handler.post_event(CustomEvent(1, value)) def callback(event: CustomEvent): print(f"the event value is {event.value}") event_generator = CustomEventGenerator() event_generator.event_handler.add_subscription(1, callback) # this gives an error My type checker (Pylance) is unhappy with: event_generator.event_handler.add_subscription(1, callback) # this gives an error Argument of type "(event: CustomEvent) -> None" cannot be assigned to parameter "callback" of type "(Event) -> None" in function "add_subscription" Type "(event: CustomEvent) -> None" is not assignable to type "(Event) -> None" Parameter 1: type "Event" is incompatible with type "CustomEvent" "Event" is not assignable to "CustomEvent" Why? They are both Event s. I could make EventHandler generic: from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Hashable, Callable, Protocol from abc import ABC @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) class Event(ABC): event_type: Hashable class EventHandler[E: Event]: subs: dict[Hashable, dict[int, Callable[[E], None]]] _next_id: int def __init__(self) -> None: self.subs = dict() self._next_id = 0 def add_subscription(self, event_type: Hashable, callback: Callable[[E], None]) -> int: self._next_id += 1 if not event_type in self.subs: self.subs[event_type] = dict() self.subs[event_type][self._next_id] = callback return self._next_id def post_event(self, event: E): for callback in self.subs[event.event_type].values(): callback(event) @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) class CustomEvent(Event): event_type: int value: float class CustomEventGenerator: event_handler : EventHandler[CustomEvent] def __init__(self) -> None: self.event_handler = EventHandler() def emit_event(self, value: float): self.event_handler.post_event(CustomEvent(1, value)) def callback(event: CustomEvent): print(f"the event value is {event.value}") event_generator = CustomEventGenerator() event_generator.event_handler.add_subscription(1, callback) That makes the type checker happy, but each time I add an EventHandler to a class I have to parameterize it. This is tedious especially for classes that can generate several different events: event_handler: EventHandler[ThisEvent | ThatEvent | AnotherEvent | YetAnotherEvent | AreYouKiddingMeEvent] and because the EventHandler doesn't need to know which events it is handling. I did try to make Event a protocol but that gives the same error. @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) class Event(Protocol): event_type: Hashable Is there a better way? Is it better to define callbacks like this? def callback(event: Event): assert(isinstance(event, CustomEvent)) print(f"the event value is {event.value}") It just seems silly to me to have to add runtime instructions to satisfy a static type checker. Python 3.14.6 Pylance 2026.3.1

title: CBC solver reports "optimal" solution but pyomo model variables are `None` valued
text:
CBC solver reports "optimal" solution but pyomo model variables are `None` valued

I came across this problem while using the oemof.solph Python package but I think the root cause is in Pyomo. The problem is a simple energy system model with storage which seeks an optimal supply-demand solution with a constraint. I got Claude to produce a minimum reproducible example (the real problem in oemof.solph is more complex): import pyomo.environ as po DEMAND = [13.897, 16.26] SOURCE_CAPACITY = 4.419 * 1.002 + 10.649 * 1.002 STORAGE_CAPACITY = 187.176 * 1.002 INITIAL_STORAGE_LEVEL = 0.06343767352673378 MIN_STORAGE_LEVEL = 13.086996442132152 # binding; 0.0 does not reproduce it LOSS_RATE = 0.001 COST = 1.1 storage_flow_cap = STORAGE_CAPACITY / 24 content0 = INITIAL_STORAGE_LEVEL * STORAGE_CAPACITY m = po.ConcreteModel() m.T = po.RangeSet(0, 1) # intervals m.TP = po.RangeSet(0, 2) # timepoints (interval boundaries) m.source = po.Var(m.T, within=po.NonNegativeReals, bounds=(0, SOURCE_CAPACITY)) m.charge = po.Var(m.T, within=po.NonNegativeReals, bounds=(0, storage_flow_cap)) m.discharge = po.Var(m.T, within=po.NonNegativeReals, bounds=(0, storage_flow_cap)) m.content = po.Var(m.TP, within=po.NonNegativeReals, bounds=(0, STORAGE_CAPACITY)) m.storage_losses = po.Var(m.T, within=po.NonNegativeReals) m.balance = po.Constraint( m.T, rule=lambda m, t: m.source[t] - m.charge[t] + m.discharge[t] == DEMAND[t] ) m.losses_def = po.Constraint( m.T, rule=lambda m, t: m.storage_losses[t] == m.content[t] * LOSS_RATE ) m.content_recursion = po.Constraint( m.T, rule=lambda m, t: m.content[t + 1] == m.content[t] - m.storage_losses[t] + m.charge[t] - m.discharge[t], ) m.initial_content = po.Constraint(expr=m.content[0] == content0) m.min_level = po.Constraint(expr=m.content[1] >= MIN_STORAGE_LEVEL) m.obj = po.Objective(expr=COST * sum(m.source[t] for t in m.T), sense=po.minimize) solver = po.SolverFactory("cbc", solver_io="lp") results = solver.solve(m, tee=False) print(f"termination_condition: {results.solver.termination_condition}") all_vars = list(m.component_data_objects(po.Var, active=True)) none_vars = [v for v in all_vars if v.value is None] print(f"variables with no value: {len(none_vars)} / {len(all_vars)}") Output: termination_condition: optimal variables with no value: 11 / 11 So the solver (CBC) has reported that it found an optimal solution but none of the decision variables have a value. What could the cause of this be? One more thing we discovered. Changing CBC's "primalTolerance" parameter does affect whether this problem occurs. solver.solve(m, options={"primalTolerance": "1e-9"}) # tighter than the gap # -> correctly reports infeasible solver.solve(m, options={"primalTolerance": "1e-5"}) # looser than the gap # -> solves cleanly, every variable has a value solver.solve(m) # CBC's default, 1e-7 # -> optimal, but 11/11 variables have no value Environment: pyomo 6.10.1, CBC 2.10.11 (also confirmed on CBC 2.10.13).

title: GStreamer later version seems to mis-identify the prepare-window-handle message
text:
GStreamer later version seems to mis-identify the prepare-window-handle message

We had some Python code that was working fine with GStreamer 1.26 but appears broken in 1.28. The code is in the bus sync handler where we expect the prepare-window-handle from our xvimagesink sink to be delivered when needed. The code we had for detecting it was: def on_sync_message(self, _, message): struct = message.get_structure() print(type(struct)) print(struct) print(bool(struct)) if struct: name = struct.get_name() print(f"Sync msg '{name}', type = {message.type}") if name == "prepare-window-handle": if self.window_id: print(f"Setting window handle to {self.window_id}") imagesink = message.src imagesink.set_window_handle(self.window_id) else: print(f"Window handle msg received") self.window_handle_set = True else: print(f"Sync msg (no structure), type = {message.type}") and that appears to be the right way to do it based on web searches and the GStreamer docs. The upshot is that, without this, the image sink opens its own fully decorated window rather than rendering into the Tk frame it used to. I originally considered a timing issue re starting the pipeline before attaching to the bus but that turned out to be false. The pipeline is created, and the bus attached to, well before setting the pipeline state to playing . In any case, the output of those print statement (the ones at the start were added for debugging) are: <class 'gi.overrides.Gst.Structure'> prepare-window-handle; False Sync msg (no structure), type = 32768 <class 'gi.overrides.Gst.Structure'> have-window-handle, window-handle=(guint64)29360130; True Sync msg 'have-window-handle', type = 32768 So, for some reason, it looks like the prepare-window-handle is arriving but being treated as a false value in the context of the if (and the bool cast). That explains why it no longer renders to the Tk frame. On a 1.26 system, the output for prepare-window-handle is different: <class 'gi.overrides.Gst.Structure'> prepare-window-handle; True I was wondering whether it's being treated as Falsey because it has no payload (unlike the have-window-handle one, which carries a handle). But I'm having a hard time tracking through the source code for Python bindings and underlying C code. So I thought I'd ask here to see if anyone has had similar issues, or whether someone more knowledgeable about GStreamer internals has some advice. Is there some newer method other than the bool-ification of the structure by which we should detect a valid message?

title: Using ast.parse to evaluate arithmetic expression safely
text:
Using ast.parse to evaluate arithmetic expression safely

_OPS = { ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul, ast.Div: operator.truediv, ast.Pow: operator.pow, ast.USub: operator.neg, ast.UAdd: operator.pos, ast.Mod: operator.mod, } def _eval(node): if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)): return node.value if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp): return _OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.left), _eval(node.right)) if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp): return _OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.operand)) if ( isinstance(node, ast.Call) and isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "log" and not node.keywords ): return math.log(*[_eval(arg) for arg in node.args]) raise ValueError(f"Unsupported expression node: {ast.dump(node)}") def evaluate(expression: str) -> float: """Safely evaluate an arithmetic expression. Supports + - * / ** % log() and parentheses.""" tree = ast.parse(expression, mode="eval") return _eval(tree.body) Given my Python implementation, I want to create an eval function for my AI agent to run calculation and eval. My approach is like this: First parse the expression into an AST, then walk the tree and execute binary or unary operations recursively until we hit a literal. title: How can I prevent duplicate Celery tasks when a FastAPI endpoint is retried?
text:
How can I prevent duplicate Celery tasks when a FastAPI endpoint is retried?

I'm using FastAPI + Celery + Redis + PostgreSQL for a document-processing workflow. A FastAPI endpoint creates a processing job and then sends a Celery task: @app.post("/reports/{report_id}/process") async def process_report(report_id: int, db: Session = Depends(get_db)): job = ProcessingJob( report_id=report_id, status="queued" ) db.add(job) db.commit() db.refresh(job) process_report_task.delay(job.id) return {"job_id": job.id} The problem is that if the client retries the request because of a timeout or network issue, multiple ProcessingJob records and multiple Celery tasks can be created for the same report. I need the operation to behave idempotently: POST /reports/123/process POST /reports/123/process POST /reports/123/process should result in only one active processing job for report 123 . I considered: Checking for an existing queued/running job before inserting Using a Redis distributed lock Adding a PostgreSQL unique constraint Passing an idempotency key from the client A simple application-level check seems vulnerable to race conditions when two requests arrive at almost the same time. For example: existing = ( db.query(ProcessingJob) .filter( ProcessingJob.report_id == report_id, ProcessingJob.status.in_(["queued", "running"]) ) .first() ) if existing: return {"job_id": existing.id} Two concurrent requests can both pass this check before either transaction inserts the new row. What is the recommended way to make this workflow idempotent? Specifically, should this be enforced primarily at the PostgreSQL level, Redis/Celery level, or through an API idempotency key? I also need to allow the same report to be processed again after the previous job reaches completed or failed . Stack: FastAPI SQLAlchemy PostgreSQL Celery Redis

title: Python match-case vs. dictionary performance internals
text:
Python match-case vs. dictionary performance internals

When conditional branching logic grows large in Python, the go-to advice has always been to map keys to functions or values using a dictionary lookup mapping.get(key) to achieve O(1) time complexity, rather than using very long, O(n) sequence of if - elif statements. However, with structural pattern matching ( match - case ) in Python 3.10+, the syntax looks pretty clean for these types of large branch choices: match status_code: case 200: return "OK" case 404: return "Not Found" case 500: return "Internal Server Error" # ... dozens of cases Does the compiler optimize a match - case block with literal values into a jump table or an internal hash map lookup, or does it evaluate sequentially like a traditional if - elif loop? Does match - case create any transient runtime overhead compared to keeping a persistent dictionary configuration in memory? I want to see how Python's internal logic handles these options when your code scales up.
